request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

A model with clear role-specific behavior such as coordination, join/leave, braking, warning, or recovery can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 if those main scenarios are present and behaviorally plausible. The normalized summary may contain [initial] pseudostates and [action] nodes; do not count those conventions as syntax problems by themselves. Score below 0.50 mainly when the behavior collapses into generic placeholder loops, the major scenarios are not recognizable, or the causal chain is seriously under-modeled.

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

review_result.overall_reason_text: The model captures the main architecture-level story: danger detection feeds a chassis safety controller, which commands chassis/powertrain actions and sends data to a communication unit that broadcasts via DSRC. It loses credit because many required constraints are not modeled at all, especially false-message prevention, fault detectability, privacy/security, congestion control, and timing. Clarity is also reduced by attribute-heavy blocks, duplicated/odd signal structure, and an apparently artificial "exchanges" block. Final overall score blended LLM judgement (0.25) with a deterministic architecture-oriented reviewer (0.75) for stability.

However, the notation quality is weakened by odd structural elements such as an "exchanges" block and duplicated/out-of-place signals that make the model look only partially disciplined as a TTool/AVATAR block diagram.

But many explicit requirements are absent from the architecture, especially single-fault detectability and false-message prevention, congestion-control and highest-priority broadcast handling, privacy/security handling, and the stated delay/security-overhead constraints.

It loses credit because many required constraints are not modeled at all, especially false-message prevention, fault detectability, privacy/security, congestion control, and timing. Clarity is also reduced by attribute-heavy blocks, duplicated/odd signal structure, and an apparently artificial "exchanges" block. Final overall score blended LLM judgement (0.25) with a deterministic architecture-oriented reviewer (0.75) for stability.

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

review_result.prompt: You are simulating a practical human review of state-machine behavior models. Score on 0.0 to 1.0. At this abstraction level, give strong credit when the main operational scenarios are recognizable through domain-specific states and transitions across the important roles, even if some timing details, quantitative constraints, or secondary edge cases are only implicit. A model with clear role-specific behavior such as coordination, join/leave, braking, warning, or recovery can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 if those main scenarios are present and behaviorally plausible. The normalized summary may contain [initial] pseudostates and [action] nodes; do not count those conventions as syntax problems by themselves. Score below 0.50 mainly when the behavior collapses into generic placeholder loops, the major scenarios are not recognizable, or the causal chain is seriously under-modeled.
review_result.overall_reason_text: The model gets partial credit because several key roles from the scenario are present as separate blocks, and there is some recognizable danger-to-warning flow through ChassisSafetyController and CommunicationUnit. However, much of the behavior collapses into generic Idle/Processing/State1/State2 patterns, and major required properties such as false-message prevention, fault detectability, congestion-control broadcasting, privacy, and timing are not behaviorally modeled. As a result, the artifact is more structurally suggestive than specification-grounded.

dimension_results.title: Notation and Syntax
dimension_results.reason_text: The artifact is recognizably organized as multiple AVATAR/TTool-style state machines with blocks, states, signals, and transitions, so it earns solid syntax credit. Initial pseudostates and action nodes are used in a generally coherent way. It loses points because some state machines are extremely schematic and contain transitions whose events/guards are not well disciplined semantically, which weakens confidence that the notation is being used meaningfully rather than just formally.

request.prompt: You are simulating a practical human review of a high-level architecture/block diagram. Score on 0.0 to 1.0. Use generous but disciplined credit for architecture-level adequacy: if the main actors/subsystems are present and the end-to-end interaction story is recognizable, the model can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 even when some detailed constraints, data abstractions, or supporting mechanisms are imperfect or implicit. Subtract moderately for extra data-holder blocks, noisy attributes, duplicated interfaces, or exceeding the requested block count. Subtract heavily only when the main architectural flow is broken, key participants are absent, or exchanges are implausible.
request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements
- No warning message without a real danger is allowed
- No failure in any single unit may be succeeded by a false message
- No failure of any single communication may be succeeded by a false message
- Any single fault in an ECU has to be detectable
- Information about dangerous events has to be broadcast according to the communica-
tion congestion control algorithms
- Information about the dangers have to be broadcast to other cars with highest priority
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed
Technical Requirements
- The maximum delay from danger detection to broadcast of the car2X message should
be less than 150 ms
- Additional security information on the busses in the chassis and safety & powertrain
domains should be less than 15% of the net data
Security aspects
- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

Use between 4 and 10 blocks

request.prompt: You are simulating a practical human review of state-machine behavior models. Score on 0.0 to 1.0. At this abstraction level, give strong credit when the main operational scenarios are recognizable through domain-specific states and transitions across the important roles, even if some timing details, quantitative constraints, or secondary edge cases are only implicit. A model with clear role-specific behavior such as coordination, join/leave, braking, warning, or recovery can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 if those main scenarios are present and behaviorally plausible. The normalized summary may contain [initial] pseudostates and [action] nodes; do not count those conventions as syntax problems by themselves. Score below 0.50 mainly when the behavior collapses into generic placeholder loops, the major scenarios are not recognizable, or the causal chain is seriously under-modeled.
request.input_text:
When a dangerous situation occurs that forces the driver, or the car itself, to perform a
manoeuvre, this can endanger other vehicles. In order to warn other vehicles, the car sends
out a warning message. Nearby cars that are in danger can then react according to the
information provided within the message.
An ECU of the chassis & safety domain detects a danger; this may be the trigger of an airbag,
an obstacle in direction of travel seen by an environmental sensor, or an emergency braking
performed by the driver or an automatic system. The Chassis Safety Controller (CSC) gets
information about the dangerous situation via the Chassis Domain Bus. The CSC will assess
the situation and will take measures to mitigate the danger for the car. The measures will
result in commands to actuator ECUs in the chassis & safety domain and additionally com-
mands to the powertrain domain to get a helpful driving power adjustment. In parallel it
will also send information to the Communication Unit (CU). This information will contain
data about the current vehicle dynamic status and detailed information about the planned
actions (deceleration or acceleration, steering, etc.).
The CU will send out a warning message that contains this information via the DSRC interface to nearby vehicles. The emergency message contains longitude, latitude, altitude,
speed, acceleration and heading of the car, the time of message generation, the expiry time
of the message, an indicator for the reliability of the information, a code that is classifying
the car, an id that is identifying the sender of the message, an event code that is classifying
the emergency situation and the planed acceleration and heading. All this information is
packed in a message frame that adds checksum, information for protocol processing and if
necessary security information.

Functional requirements

- Privacy of the broadcast car information has to be guaranteed

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

Use generous but disciplined credit for architecture-level adequacy: if the main actors/subsystems are present and the end-to-end interaction story is recognizable, the model can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 even when some detailed constraints, data abstractions, or supporting mechanisms are imperfect or implicit. request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
Platooning is a transportation technique that consists in grouping trucks or vehicles together to reduce CO2 emissions. A platoon consists of one or several vehicles, the first one in the platoon playing the role of the platoon leader, the other ones playing the role of followers.

1. A vehicle can  create a platoon: this vehicle is then the leader of this platoon. This vehicle informs neighbour cars about this platoon by sending a platoon information message (position, speed, acceleration) every second. Once followers have joined, it regularly informs ---every half second --- the followers of its current situation (speed, acceleration, direction, selected lane). Whenever there is an important modification of speed / acceleration / direction / lane, the leader immediately informs the followers. 
 
2. A follower can join a platoon only at the last position, i.e. behind all other vehicles of the platoon. When it joins the platoon, it informs the leader about this. When a follower wishes to leave the platoon, it informs all other vehicles of the platoon (with a "leave" message) and  then brakes or changes of lane.
  
3. Leaders and followers use front and back cameras to detect the lanes and the distance to other vehicles. The distance between vehicles within a platoon is considered to be between a min and a max distance. If there is less than the min distance between two vehicles, then the first vehicle detecting this situation broadcasts the information to all others and all vehicles of the platoon must perform an emergency braking. If the distance between two vehicles v1 and v2 ---with v1 before v2--- gets over max, then v2 and all the vehicles behind v2 have to leave the platoon. v2 is assumed to send the "leave" message. Obviously, one important goal of the platooning software is to keep the inter-vehicle distance between min and max so as to ensure that the platoon works for a long time. 

In a more advanced version of the platooning system, the platoon can split i.e. a given follower can decide to become the leader of all the followers behind it.

Use at least 2 blocks and at most 10 blocks.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

However, important required content is absent or under-modeled: 3D position is missing, the answer should be explicitly enciphered before TM transmission, and key watchdog/CRC constraints are only partially reflected.

evidence.snippet: Required data: "3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity"; also "answer packet ... first enciphered and then sent via a TM"
evidence.explanation: These are explicit requirement items that should be directly visible in the architecture.

evidence.snippet: GroundStation attributes include "temperature", "batteryLevel", "fuelQuantity"; blocks include "DecipherSoftware", "IntermediateBuffer", "TaskHandler", "RFSender", "Microcontroller", "WatchdogTask"
evidence.explanation: This supports substantial coverage of the required architecture, but the listed telemetry attributes omit 3D position and no dedicated encipher/send step is clearly shown.

issues.element_text: 3D position among monitored safety data
issues.reason_text: The model includes temperature, battery level, and fuel quantity, but no clear representation of 3D position.

issues.element_text: Answer packet is enciphered before TM transmission
issues.reason_text: A deciphering block exists, but no equally clear enciphering function is shown on the TM production path.

dimension_results.title: Behavioral Consistency
dimension_results.reason_text: The high-level interaction story is broadly plausible, but several required trigger-condition-effect relations are not preserved clearly enough. In particular, the latest-TC-cancels-current-TM behavior, periodic 10ms watchdog checking with restart on non-response, and CRC compute/store/check on every memory write/read are not modeled with enough behavioral specificity to trust the logic.

evidence.snippet: "while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received... TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent"
evidence.explanation: This is a concrete behavioral rule that requires clear causal logic, not just presence of generic request/response blocks.

evidence.snippet: DecipherSoftware has "responseCancelled()" and Microcontroller/WatchdogTask blocks exist, but precomputed context shows state_count=0, transition_count=0
evidence.explanation: Some names hint at the behavior, but the absence of explicit control logic means the required sequencing and restart conditions are not demonstrably preserved.

issues.element_text: New TC cancels TM under construction and replaces it
issues.reason_text: A cancellation signal exists, but the architecture does not clearly show the condition, target, and recomputation flow needed to preserve this behavior.

issues.element_text: 10ms watchdog polling/restart and CRC on every write/read
issues.reason_text: The model names related blocks/signals, but does not make the trigger/effect logic explicit enough to confirm correct behavior.

dimension_results.reason_text: The decomposition is understandable at a glance and follows the major functional pipeline of the described system. But clarity is reduced by noisy attributes, duplicated interface names, and some questionable responsibility placement, such as putting monitored data attributes on GroundStation rather than clearly modeling them as sensed spacecraft data.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_1 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including temperature.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_2 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including GroundStation.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_3 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including SpaceBasedSystem.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Data of TCs are ciphered.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_4 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including cipheredData.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_5 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including cipheredData.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_6 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including requestedValues.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_7 is supported by 7 predicted element(s), including GroundStation.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_8 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including SpaceBasedSystem.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: For this, a signal is sent to each task.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_9 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including TaskHandler.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_10 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including batteryLevel.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of the system.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_11 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including SpaceBasedSystem.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_12 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including SpaceBasedSystem.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: No clear predicted element could be traced to requirement req_13; this likely indicates an omission or a naming mismatch.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_14 is supported by 4 predicted element(s), including SpaceBasedSystem.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: No clear predicted element could be traced to requirement req_15; this likely indicates an omission or a naming mismatch.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: No clear predicted element could be traced to requirement req_16; this likely indicates an omission or a naming mismatch.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_17 is supported by 8 predicted element(s), including cipheredData.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: Requirement req_18 is supported by 3 predicted element(s), including cRCReading().

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

requirement_trace_results.reason_text: No clear predicted element could be traced to requirement req_15; this likely indicates an omission or a naming mismatch.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform.
requirement_trace_results.reason_text: No clear predicted element could be traced to requirement req_16; this likely indicates an omission or a naming mismatch.

requirement_trace_results.requirement_text: Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

request.prompt: You are simulating a practical human review of state-machine behavior models. Score on 0.0 to 1.0. At this abstraction level, give strong credit when the main operational scenarios are recognizable through domain-specific states and transitions across the important roles, even if some timing details, quantitative constraints, or secondary edge cases are only implicit. A model with clear role-specific behavior such as coordination, join/leave, braking, warning, or recovery can still deserve roughly 0.75 to 0.90 if those main scenarios are present and behaviorally plausible. The normalized summary may contain [initial] pseudostates and [action] nodes; do not count those conventions as syntax problems by themselves. Score below 0.50 mainly when the behavior collapses into generic placeholder loops, the major scenarios are not recognizable, or the causal chain is seriously under-modeled.
request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.

request.input_text:
A ground station needs to regularly monitor the safety data of a space-based system: 3D position, temperature, battery level, fuel quantity. For this, a ground station can send, via radio-frequencies, a TC (TeleCommand) to the space-based system. Once received by the RF receiver, the software of the space-based system gets the request for information. Data of TCs are ciphered. Once the software has deciphered data, it stores data in an intermediate buffer, and a task to handle this request is triggered. This task builds the answer by reading requested values from sensors. Once the answer packet has been built, it is first enciphered and then sent via a TM (TeleMetry) to the ground station, using the RF transmitter. To ensure that the system does not crash, a microcontroller of this system is dedicated to execute a software task that checks, every 10ms, that all other software tasks of the space-based embedded system are still responsive. For this, a signal is sent to each task. If some of the tasks have not responded to this signal, then the whole system is restarted, apart from the watchdog: the latter is not expected to crash, apart if the battery is too low to power the microcontroller. Obviously, this watchdog task is of prime importance for this reliability of
the system. Sometimes, while the software system is computing a TM, another TC is received. To avoid redundancy, the TM under construction is canceled: a new TM corresponding to the latest TC is computed and sent. Last but not least, space-based systems are not well protected against high-energy particles. Such a particle can provoke a bit flip from 0 to 1, or the opposite. The memory is the most sensitive elements of the platform. Therefore, for each block of data the software writes into memory, an error correction code (CRC) of this block has to be computed by the software and stored into memory along with the data block. When this block is read, the corresponding CRC must also be read and checked.
